title: Keep the workload steady

blocks.text: A water utility relines its old mains with one contractor, who has asked for a steady workload: the crews and the lining plant cost money to stand up and stand down. The contract says that from one year of the plan to the next, the utility's total relining spend may rise or fall by at most `max_step`. The model in `steady.py` already has the start variables, a row saying each project starts at most once, and `yearly_spend`, which builds each year's spend as an expression.

Write `add_steady_spend(model, spend, years, max_step)`, adding the rows that keep this rule. `spend[y]` is year `y`'s expression and `years` are the plan's years in order. Spend before the first year or after the last is not part of the rule.
The model so far, with $`P`$ the projects, $`T_i`$ the years project $`i`$ may start in, $`Y`$ the plan's years, $`c_{i,k}`$ what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work and $`S`$ the step:

Write your rows in this notation first, each with its quantifier and a label, then code them. A solver row is linear: it cannot take an absolute value, so think about what "rise or fall by at most $`S`$" says as plain inequalities.
The tests fix a schedule by setting the variables' bounds and ask the solver whether it is allowed, so any correct formulation passes. About four lines.

cases.says: a plan whose yearly spend changes by less than the step is allowed, and one that rises by more is refused
a fall in spend larger than the step is refused, not only a rise
a slow ramp whose total change exceeds the step is allowed, because each year is compared with the one before
a jump between the plan's last two years is refused
a change of exactly the step is allowed
